lesson.title: Load Resistance and the Cost of Drawing Power
lesson.summary: Load resistance is the resistance of whatever device is connected across a circuit's output terminals, and its value relative to the circuit's Thevenin resistance decides how much voltage survives and how much power actually gets delivered.
lesson.body:
Load resistance, usually written R_L, is the resistance of whatever external device is connected across a circuit's output terminals to actually use the power or signal that circuit provides. It sits on the consuming side of a connection, as opposed to a source's own internal resistance, which sits on the supplying side. The two resistances are easy to confuse because they play against each other in the exact same equation, but they describe fundamentally different physical things: one belongs to the device doing the driving, and the other belongs to the device doing the drawing.

This is where the Thevenin equivalent becomes genuinely useful rather than just a reduction exercise. Any linear two terminal resistive network, no matter how complicated internally, can be replaced by a single equivalent voltage source V_th in series with a single equivalent resistance R_th. Once you attach a load resistance R_L across those two terminals, the entire circuit collapses into one simple series loop, and Ohm's law gives you everything: the current is I = V_th divided by (R_th plus R_L), and the voltage actually delivered to the load is V_L = I times R_L.

Take a Thevenin equivalent with V_th = 12V and R_th = 4 ohm, and attach a load R_L = 4 ohm, matching the source resistance exactly. The current is I = 12V divided by (4 ohm plus 4 ohm), or 12 divided by 8, which is 1.5A. The load voltage is 1.5A times 4 ohm, or 6V, and the power delivered to the load is P = I squared times R_L, or 1.5 squared times 4, which is 9W.

Now compare two mismatched loads. With R_L = 2 ohm, the current is 12 divided by 6, or 2A, and the power is 2 squared times 2, or 8W. With R_L = 8 ohm, the current is 12 divided by 12, or 1A, and the power is 1 squared times 8, also 8W. Both mismatched cases deliver less power than the matched case, 8W instead of 9W, which is the numeric signature of the maximum power transfer theorem: power delivered to a load is maximized exactly when R_L equals R_th, and it falls off symmetrically as R_L moves away from that value in either direction.

It is worth noticing the trade off hiding in these numbers. At the matched load, only 6V out of the available 12V actually reaches the load, the other 6V is lost as heat inside R_th itself, so only half the power the source generates ends up useful. Applications that care about maximum power transfer, like audio amplifiers driving speakers or RF transmitters driving antennas, deliberately match R_L to R_th despite that loss. Applications that care about efficiency instead, like power distribution wiring, do the opposite on purpose, choosing R_L much larger than R_th so that nearly all the delivered voltage, and nearly all the power, ends up in the load rather than wasted internally.

Load resistance is not always a single fixed part either. A dimmer switch, a volume knob, or a variable test load all present a load resistance that changes continuously across a range, and the same V_th, R_th equation still applies at every setting, which is why a Thevenin equivalent is such a durable way to describe a source: it lets you predict behavior for any load resistance you might connect, not just one. Recognizing what counts as the load resistance in a given problem, the resistance of the thing actually consuming power, as distinct from any resistance that belongs to the source's own internal wiring, is the key skill this chapter builds toward, and it is exactly the distinction the later chapters on input resistance, output resistance, and loading effect depend on.
